I would keep it simple and follow the cropping pattern I trust most for Quzhou County. I would plant winter wheat first and then summer maize on the same land, because that is the most familiar, stable, and practical way for me to use the full year. At my age, I would avoid crops that need too much delicate field work or too much market gambling. I would use improved or hybrid seed where it helps yield and standability, but I would still manage the land in a straightforward way: plough or rotary tillage before wheat, return straw if possible, put most fertilizer in as base fertilizer, then topdress nitrogen once or twice, irrigate at the key stages, and spray only when disease, weeds, or insects are likely to reduce yield. For wheat, I would focus on strong seedling establishment, winter survival, spring fertilizer, and irrigation around jointing and grain filling. After harvest, I would move quickly into summer maize, use hybrid seed, keep the stand even, fertilize early, irrigate when summer rain is not enough, and control weeds and borers in time. This is the plan I would choose because it matches local conditions, spreads work across the year, and gives me the most dependable grain output.
